lessons.theory:
## What you will learn
Animation communicates movement through timed changes of pose and spacing. The classical principles—anticipation, squash and stretch, arcs, slow in/out and follow-through—make the motion readable and believable.

## Studio practice: Principles of Animation

## Animation is controlled change over time
Animation works when a viewer perceives successive frames as continuous movement. Good animation communicates a clear intention: what changed, why, how long it took and where the viewer should look. Draw a *key pose* for the most important state, add an in-between pose and check whether the sequence reads clearly without dialogue.

### Important animation principles
**Squash and stretch** suggests weight and flexibility while often preserving perceived volume. **Anticipation** prepares an audience for a movement (a character bends before jumping). **Staging** makes the main action unambiguous. **Slow in/slow out** means objects spend more frames near the beginning/end of a movement, unlike constant linear motion. **Arcs** make organic movement feel natural. **Follow-through and overlapping action** allow connected parts to settle at different times.

### Timing versus spacing
Timing means how many frames an action takes. Spacing means how far the object travels between frames. With the same duration, closely clustered poses near the end create deceleration; evenly spaced poses create constant speed. At 24 frames per second, a motion spanning 12 frames takes half a second; at 30fps, the same 12 frames take 0.4 seconds. State the playback frame rate when comparing frame counts.

### A bouncing ball
Draw a ball above the ground, mid-air, touching the floor (squashed) and rising again (stretched slightly). Keep the path on an arc and add more drawings near the peak, fewer during fast falling. For a heavy ball use less squash; for rubber use more. Do not randomly increase squash independently of motion direction.

## Key ideas made clear
- Timing is the number of frames an action lasts; spacing is the distance between successive drawings.
- Squash and stretch communicates flexibility and weight, while keeping an object’s apparent volume reasonably consistent.
- Anticipation prepares viewers for an action; for example, a character bends before jumping.
- Slow-in/slow-out clusters positions near rest and spaces them farther apart during faster movement.
- Follow-through and overlapping action make secondary parts settle later than the main body.

## Studio task
1. Sketch a ball bounce with changing spacing.
2. Explain why a heavy ball and a rubber ball squash differently.

## Frequent production errors
- Using uniform frame spacing for a motion that should accelerate.
- Exaggerating squash without considering material stiffness and mass.
- Treating anticipation as unnecessary delay instead of communicating intent.
- Changing the FPS without retiming frame counts.

workedExamples.title: Plan a one-second bounce
workedExamples.problem: Create a 24fps ball bounce and show weight clearly.
workedExamples.solution: Frame 1: high pose; 6: descending; 10: just above ground; 12: contact with squash; 14: rising; 20: slower near peak; 24: hold or transition. Keep a consistent arc and add easing by varying spacing.
workedExamples.explanation: The number of frames controls duration, while inter-frame distance explains speed and acceleration.

lessons.theory:
## What you will learn
2D animation production moves from storyboard and animatic to key poses, breakdowns, in-betweens, cleanup, colouring and export. Organised layers and consistent frame rate are essential.

## Studio practice: 2D Animation Tools

## A practical 2D production pipeline
Begin with a short storyboard showing the camera framing and key actions. Create an animatic (timed rough storyboard with temporary sound) before spending time on polished artwork. Next draw key poses, extremes and breakdown poses. Add in-betweens, clean line art, colour, effects and sound. Finally export and verify playback.

### Timeline, layers and keyframes
A timeline arranges frames or keyframes in time. Layers separate background, character, effects and audio, making edits easier. Onion-skinning temporarily shows earlier and later drawings with reduced opacity so you can keep spacing and volumes consistent.

### Frame-by-frame versus tweening
Frame-by-frame animation offers fine expressive control because each pose is drawn. Tweening/interpolation creates in-between positions, opacity changes or transforms from keyframes and works well for simple vector/UI motion. A combination is often most efficient. Interpolation does not remove the need for good key poses and easing curves.

### Common mistakes
If the character flickers, check shape consistency and registration between frames. If movement feels robotic, revise timing and spacing instead of adding more drawings at uniform intervals. If export stutters, verify project frame rate, export frame rate and that the animation's duration has not been trimmed.

### File and export choices
Preserve an editable project file with separate layers. Export PNG sequences when transparency or post-production flexibility is important. Use MP4/H.264 for a common delivery format when transparency is not required; GIF is limited in colours and is less suitable for large high-quality scenes.

## Key ideas made clear
- A storyboard defines shot order, composition and the intent of each movement before detailed drawing.
- An animatic adds timing and temporary audio to storyboards so pacing problems are caught early.
- Key poses establish the action; breakdowns clarify the path; in-betweens complete smooth movement.
- Onion skin displays adjacent frames to keep character proportions, registration and arcs consistent.
- Tweening interpolates simple transforms; frame-by-frame drawing gives more control over expressive poses.

## Studio task
1. Label a four-stage storyboard-to-export pipeline.
2. Explain when a hand wave needs frame-by-frame drawing rather than simple tweening.

## Frequent production errors
- Polishing artwork before validating the animatic timing.
- Using random layer names so assets cannot be edited safely.
- Assuming automatic tweening creates convincing anticipation or weight.
- Exporting at a different frame rate without checking duration.

lessons.theory:
## What you will learn
3D animation begins with geometry, materials, camera and lighting. A rig gives mesh objects an articulated structure so transform keyframes can produce controlled motion.

## Studio practice: 3D Modeling Basics

## Build a 3D object from geometry
A polygon mesh contains vertices (points), edges (connections) and faces (surfaces). Start with simple primitives—cube, cylinder, sphere—and use operations such as extrusion, inset, loop cuts and beveling to develop form. Keep geometry appropriate to the task: highly detailed meshes require more memory and processing.

### Object transformations
Translation changes position, rotation changes orientation and scaling changes size. The common coordinate axes are X, Y and Z. Local transformations operate relative to an object's orientation; global transformations use world axes. Before rigging or exporting, understand whether a tool expects local or world coordinates and whether transforms need to be applied.

### Materials, lighting and camera
Geometry alone does not produce a readable final image. Materials describe surface response (colour, roughness, metallic appearance). Lights determine highlights and shadows. Camera position, focal length and composition determine what the viewer notices. A simple three-point lighting setup uses a key light, fill and rim/back light to separate form from the background.

### Animation and rigging
A rig contains bones/controllers that move mesh parts without manually editing each vertex. Keyframes store pose or transformation values at chosen times, and interpolation creates positions between them. Deformation depends on skinning weights; bad weights produce collapsing elbows or stretching faces.

### Export and optimisation
Check polygon count, texture resolution, file sizes and draw calls before putting 3D on a website. Bake details into normal maps when possible. Preview the model on the target device rather than assuming a workstation render will run smoothly on a phone.

## Key ideas made clear
- Meshes are built from vertices, edges and faces; polygon complexity determines how expensive a model is to render.
- Translation moves an object, rotation changes orientation and scaling changes size in 3D coordinates.
- Correct pivot positions are crucial: an elbow must rotate about its joint, not the mesh center.
- Materials describe surface appearance, while lighting and camera framing determine the final readable view.
- Rigging creates a bone/controller hierarchy, and skinning weights determine which vertices follow each bone.

## Studio task
1. Draw a two-bone robot arm with pivot at elbow.
2. Explain why model optimisation matters for web/mobile.

## Frequent production errors
- Placing the pivot at the wrong point and producing unnatural joint motion.
- Adding detailed polygons before the silhouette and topology are correct.
- Ignoring applied transforms when exporting to another application.
- Assuming a workstation render guarantees mobile real-time performance.

lessons.theory:
## What you will learn
SVG renders scalable vector shapes, while CSS transitions and keyframes animate their transforms, opacity and appearance. Effective UI animation should be legible, performant and respectful of reduced-motion settings.

## Studio practice: CSS and SVG Animation

## CSS motion and SVG vector graphics
A CSS transition interpolates a property when a class, pseudo-class or attribute changes. Use transitions for simple interactions such as hover, focus and expanding a card. Use `@keyframes` when the motion requires multiple stages, looping or choreography.

### Transform and performance
Animate `transform: translate/scale/rotate` and `opacity` when practical. Animating `width`, `height`, `top` and `left` can force layout recalculation. Browser rendering includes style, layout, paint and compositing; unnecessary repeated layout/paint work makes scrolling feel janky.

### SVG essentials
SVG draws vector shapes such as `<circle>`, `<rect>`, `<line>` and `<path>` inside a coordinate system controlled by `viewBox`. SVG scales without typical raster blur. Stroke-dasharray and stroke-dashoffset can create a path-drawing effect, while CSS transform can move icons or shapes.

### Reduced motion and accessibility
Decorative animation should be optional for users requesting reduced motion. Provide a `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` rule that disables transforms or long-running animation while keeping the result readable. Respect users with attention or vestibular sensitivities; avoid excessive parallax, flashing or endless bouncing.

### Practical debugging
When a shape jumps, inspect transform-origin and SVG viewBox. When the CSS animation does not start, check selector specificity, property names, animation-duration and whether an element is hidden. A slide-in element should not become keyboard-inaccessible while visually off screen.

## Key ideas made clear
- SVG's viewBox defines the internal coordinate system for scalable paths, circles and text.
- CSS transitions respond to state changes; @keyframes describes named multi-stage or looping animation.
- Transform and opacity can often be composited without changing document layout.
- transform-origin and SVG transform-box control the pivot of rotations and scales.
- prefers-reduced-motion lets viewers request less movement while retaining important state cues.

## Studio task
1. Animate only transform/opacity in a simple pulse.
2. Include a reduced-motion fallback with the same readable end state.

## Frequent production errors
- Animating left/width unnecessarily and causing layout work.
- Using an incorrect viewBox or transform origin so elements jump.
- Creating flashing or endlessly bouncing elements near readable text.
- Hiding buttons visually without managing keyboard focus.

workedExamples.title: Fix a jerky sliding navigation panel
workedExamples.problem: A side drawer animates its CSS left property and drops frames on mid-range phones.
workedExamples.solution: Position the drawer outside the viewport with transform:translateX(100%); on open, change to translateX(0). Animate transform and make controls focusable only when the drawer is open.
workedExamples.explanation: Transform animations usually avoid expensive layout work, and focus management prevents hidden controls from confusing keyboard users.

codeExamples.title: Accessible SVG loading pulse
codeExamples.code:
<svg viewBox="0 0 120 40" role="img" aria-label="Loading">
  <circle class="pulse" cx="20" cy="20" r="8"/>
  <circle class="pulse" cx="60" cy="20" r="8" style="animation-delay:.15s"/>
  <circle class="pulse" cx="100" cy="20" r="8" style="animation-delay:.3s"/>
</svg>
<style>
.pulse { fill: #6366f1; transform-box: fill-box; transform-origin: center;
         animation: pulse 900ms ease-in-out infinite alternate; }
@keyframes pulse { from { opacity:.4; transform:scale(.65) }
                  to { opacity:1; transform:scale(1) } }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .pulse { animation: none; opacity: 1; }
}
</style>
codeExamples.explanation: Three circles pulse in sequence. Reduced-motion users see stable circles instead of repeated motion.

lessons.theory:
## What you will learn
Motion graphics combine typography, vector shapes, video and sound into a timed visual explanation. Start with a script and storyboard; use keyframes, easing and readable holds to guide the viewer.

## Studio practice: Motion Graphics

## Design motion graphics for communication
Motion graphics combine typography, shapes, colour, footage and movement to communicate a message. Start from a script and storyboard. Decide the visual hierarchy: which phrase, number or image should be noticed first, and which should appear next. Motion should guide attention rather than compete with content.

### Composition and pacing
A title animation benefits from three phases: anticipation, entrance and readable hold. Avoid continuous movement when viewers need time to read technical terms. Use consistent spacing, margins, alignment and colour contrast across scenes. Motion curves make accelerations feel intentional: ease-out often suits a new element arriving, and ease-in suits a departing element.

### Keyframes and interpolation
Animate position, scale, rotation and opacity with keyframes, then refine timing with an easing graph. Motion blur may improve realism but can reduce text sharpness. For typography, avoid moving small text too quickly or animating many lines at once.

### Layer hierarchy and effects
A composition may include background, text, icons, masks, transition mattes and audio. Masks reveal/hide content without deleting it. A precomposition groups related layers into a reusable sequence. Keep layers named so edits and handoff remain manageable.

### Rendering and delivery
Choose output resolution, aspect ratio, FPS and codec based on where the video will be used. For a 1920×1080 social/product clip, H.264 MP4 is a common compatible delivery format; preserve an editable master separately. Check sound levels, trim errors, frame continuity, safe margins and playback on a real phone.

### Accessibility
Provide captions for voice-over and give key text enough on-screen time. Avoid flashing rapidly or relying on colours alone for explanation.

## Key ideas made clear
- A storyboard converts a short script into visual shots and on-screen reading order.
- Visual hierarchy makes one title, number or demonstration dominant at any instant.
- Easing curves decide how fast an element accelerates or settles between keyframes.
- Masks reveal or conceal layers without deleting the source artwork.
- Final quality checks include safe margins, readable text duration, captions, audio levels and device playback.

## Studio task
1. Plan a 10-second feature introduction with at least one reading hold.
2. Check subtitles, audio, safe margins and mobile legibility.

## Frequent production errors
- Animating several competing text lines at once.
- Keeping technical terms on screen for too few frames to read.
- Using motion blur so heavily that text is illegible.
- Exporting without checking audio, aspect ratio and frame continuity.

lessons.revisionSummary: A storyboard converts a short script into visual shots and on-screen reading order. Visual hierarchy makes one title, number or demonstration dominant at any instant. Easing curves decide how fast an element accelerates or settles between keyframes. Masks reveal or conceal layers without deleting the source artwork.
